TOKYO, Nov 25 : The US dollar took a breather on Wednesday ahead of inflation and growth data, the last major readings before a December Federal Reserve policy meeting at which traders see a 97 per cent chance of an interest rate hike. The yen held steady following figures showing Japan's service-sector prices jumped to a 36-year high in October. The Australian dollar climbed after data showing hotter-than-forecast inflation in October. Investor attention now turns to the release of US gross domestic product data for the third quarter as well as the Fed's preferred inflation gauge. The greenback gave up ground on Tuesday as concern crept back into the AI trade that has attracted vast sums of capital to the US. "The whole of November has been a really, really strong month for the US dollar," Rodrigo Catril, a senior FX strategist at the National Australia Bank, said on a podcast. "So it's a little bit of a consolidation story in currencies rather than safe haven for the US dollar as the theme."

The dollar index, which measures the greenback against six peers, was flat at 103.85 following a 0.44 per cent slide in the prior session. The euro was down 0.03 per cent at $1.0961. The yen edged 0.03 per cent lower to 159.28 a dollar, while sterling weakened 0.05 per cent to $1.3106. With no end in sight to the Middle East crisis, elevated oil prices have kept central banks in a hawkish posture to rein in inflation. Euro zone policymaker Olaf Sleijpen said on Tuesday the European Central Bank is likely to raise its policy interest rate in December, though the path after that is unclear. Fed funds futures traders are pricing in 97 per cent odds of a Fed hike in December, and a 66 per cent chance of an additional increase in January, showed the CME Group's FedWatch Tool. But with concern about the viability of the AI trade driving recent share selling, investors have begun to question how much the Fed can tighten policy without crimping the economy.  On Wednesday, the US Commerce Department is widely expected to report that the Personal Consumption Expenditures index nudged up 0.3 per cent in October, compared with a 0.5 per cent gain in the month before. The agency will also release its second estimate of GDP for the third quarter, which market participants expect to show that the economy grew at a 3.5 per cent annualised rate. In Japan, a key gauge of service-sector inflation jumped 4.2 per cent in October from a year earlier, official data showed on Wednesday, a sign of broadening price pressure that bolsters the case for a near-term interest rate hike by the central bank. Data also on Wednesday showed Australian consumer prices climbed by more than markets expected in October, while a stubbornly high reading for core inflation underlined why the policy interest rate has risen five times this year. The Australian dollar strengthened 0.29 per cent versus the greenback to $0.6657, while New Zealand's kiwi weakened 0.09 per cent to $0.5477. In cryptocurrencies, bitcoin fell 0.52 per cent to $59,507.77, while ether declined 0.54 per cent to $1,669.73.

TOKYO, Nov 25 : Japan's Nikkei share index is forecast to rise further next year but remain well below its recent record high as investors reassess AI-linked bets following the US midterm elections, a Reuters poll of equity strategists showed. The poll was conducted during extreme market volatility, with the Nikkei closing on Friday at its lowest level since mid-April on fears that potentially tougher AI regulations in the US could slow infrastructure growth that is critical to the industry. Markets were closed on Monday for a holiday. On Tuesday, the Nikkei jumped nearly 4 per cent as chip giant Nvidia reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO drove investors back into AI-related shares. The index is still down around 20 per cent from its June peak. The Nikkei index will be at 65,000 by June 2027 before rising to 67,500 by year-end, medians in the survey of 22 analysts taken between November 16 and 24 showed. The index closed at 58,644.63 on Tuesday.

"Technology shares were oversold," Hiroyuki Ueno, chief strategist at Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Asset Management, said on Friday. "Worries over a slowdown of data centre construction will ease after a new (US) Congress starts in January with a clearer picture of the regulations to be installed." The recent decline in stock prices was merely a valuation adjustment, as strong corporate earnings have already been confirmed, said Kohei Onishi, a senior investment researcher at Mitsubishi UFJ Morgan Stanley Securities.  "Once the market regains its composure, stocks are likely to be bought back to the level before the US midterm elections, with the potential for the Nikkei to reach new highs before the end of the year," he said. AI trade has driven global share indices to record highs this year, with the Nikkei reaching its all-time peak of 72,831.73 in June in a fast-paced rally. That optimism has faded as the price tag for planned infrastructure grew to ever-larger sums. "While we do not expect medium- to long-term growth expectations for AI itself to recede, the market has entered a phase of verifying whether massive AI investments will translate into actual earnings growth," said Yugo Tsuboi, chief strategist at Daiwa Securities.  The Reuters poll showed the Nikkei would grind higher to reach 69,000 by mid-2028. "The market will unlikely see the rosy sentiment we saw in May and June this year," said Hiroshi Namioka, chief strategist at T&D Asset Management. "However, as the evolution of AI can be dubbed as an industrial revolution, we view this as a development that will lead to a sustainable growth story rather than just a passing fad." TOKYO, Nov 25 : A key gauge of Japan's service-sector inflation jumped 4.2 per cent in October for the fastest annual pace since 1990, data showed on Wednesday, a sign of broadening price pressures that bolster the case for a near-term interest rate hike by the central bank. The year-on-year rise in the services producer price index, which tracks the prices companies charge each other for services, followed a revised gain of 3.8 per cent in September, data from the Bank of Japan showed. The increase was driven largely by rising costs of ocean freight transport, leasing and higher hotel charges, the data showed. The data is closely watched by the BOJ for clues to what extent companies are passing on rising labour costs to service-related prices.

BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda has signalled the bank's readiness to keep raising rates to prevent inflation from deviating above its 2 per cent target. Chinese fast-fashion giant Shein will pay US$100 million to settle with the US Federal Trade Commission over claims it misled consumers on shipping times, product reviews and the origin of cotton in some of its goods, according to court documents filed on Tuesday (Nov 24). Despite marketing fast shipping, Shein knew customers were receiving packages days or months late, and in some instances not at all, the FTC said in its complaint. The company makes up around half of fast-fashion sales in the US, t he agency said. A Shein spokesperson said the company had not admitted liability and that it disagreed with some of the FTC's claims. Shein agreed to continue strengthening its consumer practices and compliance efforts as part of the settlement, the company said. Shein also agreed not to misrepresent shipping times or block negative reviews, among other changes. The FTC , which protects consumers from unfair business practices, will use the funds to reimburse c ustomers, according to court documents . REVIEW PRACTICES AND SUSTAINABILITY CLAIMS CHALLENGED

Shein internal guidance told employees to exclude "extremely bad comments", such as that a piece of jewellery would stain the customer's skin, the FTC said. The FTC also accused Shein of making misrepresentations and unsubstantiated claims about its supply chain. Shein has long grappled with claims that its clothes contain cotton from the Xinjiang region, where the US and human rights groups say government-sponsored forced labour programs target Uyghur minorities. Shein has previously said it does not use Chinese cotton in products sold in the US, where the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act bans any imports from Xinjiang. Shein , founded in China and headquartered in Singapore, went public in September in Hong Kong. The retailer was known for selling US$5 dresses and US$10 jeans, but it has been forced to raise its prices as the US and then Europe closed customs duty loopholes.

Nov 24 : Dell Technologies on Tuesday raised its annual revenue and profit forecasts for the third time this year after record quarterly results, fueled by soaring enterprise demand for AI infrastructure. Shares of Dell were up about 5 per cent in extended trading after the company's board also approved an additional $25 billion share repurchase plan. The Texas-based company has been benefiting from the generative AI boom, as more businesses and cloud providers are buying Dell's AI servers, which are powered by Nvidia chips, to run complex AI workloads and autonomous agents. For fiscal 2027, Dell now expects revenue of $202 billion, above its prior target of $192 billion and Wall Street expectations of $194.48 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG.

Dell, meanwhile, reported slower growth in its PC business as customers prioritized spending on servers and storage. Its PC unit revenue rose 3 per cent to $12.89 billion in the third quarter ended October 30, compared with 20 per cent growth in the previous three months. Both Dell and HP warned of continued memory cost pressures, with Dell expecting the memory chip shortage to continue into 2027. Dell's Infrastructure Solutions Group, which houses its server and storage operations, largely drove the gains in the company's profit and growth, with revenue from the segment nearly tripling to $41.97 billion in the third quarter. Dell's record third-quarter revenue of $54.94 billion exceeded analysts' average estimate of $49.32 billion. Its adjusted EPS of $9.45 also topped estimates of $6.59. Clarke said demand continues to accelerate and broaden globally, with more than 7,500 customers deploying Dell AI Factories, a bundle that combines servers, storage, networking and software to help businesses build and run AI models. Dell ended the third quarter with a record $132.3 billion in AI server backlog after logging $60.2 billion in new orders during the period.

SAO PAULO, Nov 24 : When a tiny blue chick finally broke free from its shell after weeks of anxious waiting, keepers at Brazil's Sao Paulo Zoo saw more than the birth of a bird; they saw a glimmer of hope for a species that has vanished from the wild. Aptly named Hope, the female Spix's macaw born in October forms part of a breeding program aimed at rebuilding populations of one of the world's rarest parrots. Known in Brazil as the Ararinha-azul, the species became internationally famous after inspiring Blu, the main character of the 2011 animated film Rio, a domesticated Spix's macaw who embarks on a journey to save his species. "We chose 'Hope' because we hope we can give a better future to this species," said Fernanda Guida, head biologist at the zoo's bird division.

Hope's arrival followed a tense 28-day artificial incubation process. Zoo specialists removed the egg for monitoring and eventually intervened when the bird struggled to hatch. Brazil's environment ministry backs the zoo's program. "It was 28 days of suffering until we saw her hatch. She needed help, we had to remove her from inside the egg because she was badly positioned, and then she hatched," Guida said. Native to the Caatinga region of northeastern Brazil, Spix's macaws were pushed to the brink of extinction by deforestation and decades of trapping for the illegal pet trade. The species is classified as "extinct in the wild" by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List, meaning its survival has depended on captive populations. "That first hatching was a very important milestone for the conservation of the Spix's macaw," Guida said. "It's a long road ahead of us, but it's the path we hope will be very successful."

WASHINGTON, Nov 24 : The US Central Intelligence Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence recently discovered a cybersecurity breach that exposed some of their unclassified information, according to a person familiar with the matter. The intrusions affected a network that looks for intelligence insights in public, unclassified material, according to the New York Times, which first reported on the breach. While it was not clear specifically what unclassified material was compromised, information at other government agencies was also believed to have been exposed in the breach, the Times added. Asked about the report, the ODNI said there had been "no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems." The news is the latest in a series of tech outages and cybersecurity incidents, including a breach reported at the US Department of Agriculture. Two separate breaches have recently been disclosed at the FBI, while the Pentagon and the Department of Homeland Security have also been caught up in recent cyber incidents. The Times report did not say how the breach occurred.

Nov 24 : Elon Musk asked a federal appeals court to overturn a jury verdict finding he defrauded Twitter shareholders out of billions of dollars by threatening to abandon his purchase of the social media company four years ago. In a court filing on Monday night, Musk said shareholders failed to prove that Twitter's stock price fell on May 13, 2022, because he posted that the $44 billion takeover was "temporarily on hold" until Twitter demonstrated that its platform was not overrun by fake and spam accounts. Musk told the San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals that nothing linked the 9.7 per cent share price decline to $40.72 to any "material falsity" in his post, and that shareholders sought to hold him liable for securities fraud simply because the share price fell. The world's richest person also said the trial judge should not have certified a class action because many investors likely did not rely on his post when selling Twitter shares.

Nov 24 : Microsoft has declared a "Code Red" drive to overhaul how it prevents and responds to major service failures after a 24-hour outage exposed shortcomings in its engineering systems and crisis response, according to internal memos reviewed by Reuters. The November 12-13 outage hit governments from Australia and Japan to the United States, delayed trading firms and disrupted airline communications, fueling broader concerns about the vulnerability of critical digital infrastructure. Microsoft said the incident was not related to cyber activity or AI agents. Microsoft blamed the outage on an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July. CEO Satya Nadella publicly apologized for the disruption. The Code Red signified the most severe and urgent alert to address weaknesses in Microsoft's engineering and operational practices after the outage disrupted Exchange Online, its cloud-based email service, as well as Outlook, Teams, its Copilot AI assistant and other Microsoft 365 products.

It was the most customer-impacting incident in the history of Exchange Online, M365 Core President Jason Henderson said in a memo to staff on Friday. Never before had so many customers been without email for so long, he said. "Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team," Henderson added. 'FOG OF WAR' Amanda Silver, Microsoft's corporate vice president overseeing M365 Core and Work IQ, the company's workplace intelligence platform for AI agents, said in a separate memo on Monday that engineers had to work through a "fog of war" as the outage unfolded. Despite deploying top engineering personnel, responders exchanged more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats and struggled to maintain a cohesive picture of hypotheses and decisions because diagnostic data was scattered across fragmented internal tracking systems, Silver said. Charles Lamanna, Microsoft's executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, told a Code Red review that the affected component had experienced "roughly ten years' worth of acceptable failures," according to Silver's memo. "Our work doesn't end when service is restored. Our teams keep working around the clock to quickly implement any lessons learned, and our leadership makes sure this is our top priority," a company spokesperson told Reuters when contacted about the memos. RECOVERY TARGET As part of the Code Red, a high-priority mobilization reserved for critical crises, Silver outlined five workstreams focused on load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning and faster recovery mechanisms. Microsoft set a target of achieving worldwide resolution within an hour during future incidents and plans to deploy AI agents to help engineers diagnose system health data more quickly. Henderson said he would hold daily meetings with the Substrate leadership team, which oversees the engineering group responsible for underlying Microsoft 365 services, to track actions stemming from the outage, along with weekly reviews. The company spokesperson said Microsoft is committed not only to resolving issues when they occur, but to doing everything possible to prevent future disruptions. SLOW PATCH DEPLOYMENTS "Unfortunately, all the work we have done over the years was not sufficient to protect us on Thursday," Henderson said, adding that he had conducted an extensive review of the broader organizational and structural issues that allowed the failures to occur. In another memo earlier this month reviewed by Reuters, Henderson said "urgent patches to our M365 Core services" took too long to deploy worldwide. "In a separate recent incident, an urgent production fix took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. For our most urgent security issues, we need to get from detection to safe worldwide deployment in an hour. Needless to say, we aren't here yet," he wrote.

WASHINGTON, Nov 24 : A group of two dozen House Democrats on Tuesday raised serious concerns about the Federal Aviation Administration decision to deploy a new AI tool to assist air traffic controllers nationwide on November 10, days before a major system failure. The FAA in September began using a new software-based AI tool system in the Washington area that uses predictive analytics to improve how flights are managed after awarding an $875 million, 12-year contract to Air Space Intelligence. The Democrats, led by Representative Rick Larsen of Washington, the ranking member of the House Transportation Committee, criticized the "sudden expansion of a largely untested system" and asked the FAA to answer a series of questions by November 30. "We have yet to receive any substantive information proving the system was properly validated before its nationwide expansion," the lawmakers wrote. The system, dubbed Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories, or SMART, uses data to analyze airline schedules, weather, airport capacity, airspace conditions and operational constraints to predict traffic flows and identify potential conflicts before they occur.

Astronomers have now found the oldest-known quasar, one that formed so early in cosmic history that they are still trying to decipher how it happened. They identified a quasar dating to more than 13.1 billion years ago when the cosmos was less than 5 per cent of its current age, some 630 million years after the Big Bang event that initiated the universe. The quasar dates to 40 million years earlier than the previous record holder, disclosed in July.

"I think it adds to the evidence that some objects in the early universe developed remarkably quickly. Just 630 million years after the Big Bang, this black hole had already grown to about 360 million times the mass of the sun and was shining as a quasar," said astronomer Julien Wolf of the European Southern Observatory in Germany, lead author of the research published in the journal Astronomy and Astrophysics. Black holes are extraordinarily dense objects with gravity so strong that not even light can escape. The quasar was first detected by the European Space Agency's Euclid orbiting telescope and then further characterized using a combination of ground- and space-based telescopes.  The researchers gave the quasar the nickname Dún Aonghasa, the name of an ancient stone fort in Ireland that is perched atop a cliff overlooking the vast expanse of the Atlantic Ocean. A supermassive black hole that powers a quasar is typically billions of times more massive than the sun.  "As enormous amounts of gas, dust and matter fall toward the black hole, they form a swirling accretion disk that heats up to extreme temperatures and radiates tremendous amounts of energy, outshining the entire rest of the galaxy by factors of hundreds or even thousands," said astronomer and study co-author Silvia Belladitta of the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy in Germany and the INAF Bologna Observatory of Astrophysics and Space Science in Italy. "This makes quasars visible across billions of light-years, allowing us to observe them from the very early universe. Studying quasars helps astronomers understand how the first galaxies formed and evolved, and how the supermassive black holes at their hearts grew to such enormous sizes," Belladitta said. The Dún Aonghasa supermassive black hole is about 90 times more massive than the one at the center of our Milky Way. A TRANSFORMATIVE EPOCH It dates to one of the universe's most dramatic and transformative epochs. After the Big Bang, the cosmos cooled into a dark and neutral fog of hydrogen gas. The first stars and galaxies then began to ignite, and their intense radiation slowly burned through the fog, making the universe transparent to light for the first time. "This process was still unfolding at the time this quasar and its host galaxy were forming. It is a remarkable epoch to find such an object. The supermassive black hole powering this quasar had already grown to an enormous mass in an extremely short time, which challenges our understanding of how black holes can grow so large so quickly in the early universe," Belladitta said. One possibility is that this black hole started out small after the demise of a star that was part of the first stellar generation, but the observations indicated it was consuming material at a rate too slow to have achieved its great mass so quickly. Another possibility is that it may have been born big in a formation scenario called direct collapse.  "Normally, a large cloud of gas cools and breaks up into smaller clumps that form stars. Under the right conditions, the gas could stay warm enough to limit that fragmentation, allowing much of it to flow towards the center. That gas can build up a single enormous star that quickly collapses into a black hole. That black hole would start out far more massive than the remnant of a typical first-generation star," Wolf said. The researchers said Euclid may yet spot quasars at farther distances — meaning older — than Dún Aonghasa, with theoretical models suggesting that the first quasars could potentially date to 270 million to 470 million years post-Big Bang. "So in short: this is the furthest quasar we have ever seen, but maybe not the furthest there is to find," Belladitta said.

Nov 24 : Best Buy raised its annual comparable sales growth target on Tuesday, betting on robust demand during the holiday shopping season as customers spend on new AI-enabled phones and TVs as well as wearable technology such as smart glasses. "We're seeing the emerging categories bucket ... health rings, AI glasses, and trading cards and collectibles are driving about a full point of comp (comparable sales growth) for us," CEO Jason Bonfig told Reuters. Affluent consumers have been splurging on pricier nice-to-have products across categories from dual-screen phones to Coach handbags, as they lock in gains from stock market portfolios and investments in assets such as real estate. In contrast, lower- and middle-income consumers have sharply pulled back spending, with inflation and high gas prices crimping budgets, exacerbating a K-shaped effect among US consumers this year.

Best Buy said it saw "significant strength" in its business above the $1,500 price point in the three months through October, when total comparable sales jumped 6.1 per cent and handily beat estimates of 2.3 per cent growth. Best Buy now expects annual comparable sales to rise between 3.4 per cent and 4 per cent, compared with its earlier target of 1.9 per cent to 3 per cent growth. Its stock rose about 2 per cent in morning trading. Comparable sales growth driven by computing and phones is a positive sign for electronics at Walmart, Target and Costco heading into the holiday shopping season, said Stifel analyst Michael Montani. Higher memory chip costs have driven up product prices, but computing demand remained resilient, Best Buy executives said on a post-earnings call. Trade-ins on older products, credit card financing options and some promotions were levers Best Buy was pulling to support sales in the category, executives added. Best Buy's total revenue rose 5.8 per cent to $10.24 billion in the third quarter, beating estimates of $9.90 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG. As customers prepared for the launch of "Grand Theft Auto VI", the much-awaited installment in Take-Two Interactive's flagship franchise, Best Buy saw growth in gaming hardware and accessories in the third quarter, Bonfig said. The company raised its fiscal 2027 adjusted earnings per share target to between $6.90 and $7.05, after quarterly adjusted earnings of $1.62 per share topped estimates.

WASHINGTON, Nov 24 : Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh has called artificial intelligence a "hinge" of history critical to US leadership, but the technology has also become key to Fed policy as officials debate whether the AI boom is a transformational moment, a source of inflation, or the harbinger of an economic meltdown.  For Warsh, who calls himself "cautiously optimistic" about what he refers to as "super intelligence," as President Donald Trump does, it may be an all-of-the-above dilemma that challenges the US central bank and his leadership of it. "This is a serious test for Warsh," Evercore ISI Vice Chairman Krishna Guha, a former New York Fed official, wrote after major US equity indexes closed last week in correction territory. They were dragged down by nervousness about AI's ability to pay off and by unease over the scandal around AI chip giant Nvidia and the brief ouster of its CEO. Recent inflation and growth data "is too hot and too strong ... But with growth dependent on AI investment and AI consumer net-worth effects, the Fed needs any weakening to remain contained," Guha wrote. "Warsh needs to balance the data with markets that suggest the forward look is cooler, and his desire to assert inflation credibility with his desire not to go down in history as the Fed chair who blew up the AI boom."

After a run that saw a political backlash against AI, a market slump, a major initial public offering, a massive corporate scandal, and a seeming rebound from it all with equity markets again surging, Fed officials are expected to follow through with a quarter-percentage-point rate increase at their December 8-9 meeting. While they do not necessarily aim to — or have any guarantee they can — slow the AI boom, many see it pushing growth beyond potential and see the need to restrain some aspects of investment and demand. "If the investment rate slows way down, then yes, I'd be less concerned that there would be overheating in the economy," Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee told reporters last week, likening the strain AI puts on capacity to trying to get a "pig through the python." But the impact of rate hikes on the economy "doesn't have to be sector by sector," he said. "The Fed has only one tool, which is to tighten rates ... I do think data centers are included in that business investment" and might be influenced by rising borrowing costs. 'VERY TROUBLING SIGN' Some US central bank officials have recently discussed AI. Fed Governor Lisa Cook noted possible financial risks and the likelihood that AI is already eliminating jobs, and Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said AI investment is currently raising inflation, with any productivity benefits still to come. Warsh, who before taking over as Fed chief had cautioned central bankers to avoid taking sides on political issues like climate change, has called success in AI a make-or-break issue for the US.  "We are at a hinge point for the US economy, the United States' role in the world," Warsh said last week at an AI conference he commissioned, held at the San Francisco Fed. "I don't think any of us are impartial to how we want that to come out."  Increasingly, however, Warsh's colleagues see a more nuanced debate and are focused on near-term implications. The volatility has been apparent: Nvidia reversed course and rehired Jensen Huang as its chief executive officer on Monday, and stocks surged back after recent sharp losses. Politically, the country has become more divided, too, about how to balance AI's benefits and risks, the pace of construction, and concerns that the technology is moving too fast without proper oversight. "People are afraid. When the average American hears AI, they hear I'll lose my job, my kids will lose their jobs, my children's mental health, national security, some version of that," former US Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo said on a panel with Warsh at his AI conference.  Raimondo, who currently co-chairs a nonprofit trying to ease the AI transition for workers, noted that many ballot initiatives meant to slow data-center construction were approved by voters during the recent US midterm elections. "I think that is a very troubling sign," she said. "When people are afraid they say 'stop.' I think that would be very bad for America and for them. So where I think we have to go from here is to figure out how we address people's legitimate concerns." WARSH 'BROUGHT THIS REVOLT ON HIMSELF' The Fed's role, as Warsh likes to note, is not to pick winners and losers but to guide the credit conditions in which all firms operate, in ways that affect inflation. Fed officials' view of AI investment as a source of inflation has put the Fed at direct odds with Trump, who wants the boom to roll on. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other administration officials say rising prices are primarily the fault of still-high global oil prices that will fade as energy costs ease.  Warsh, who has defined his chairmanship partly by avoiding guidance on upcoming policy decisions, has acknowledged that AI "hits demand first," with supply and productivity improvements coming later and possibly helping ease inflation down the road. But he has not yet made the same leap as others and has avoided commenting on whether he feels the AI boom and inflation are now running hand in hand, and on how the Fed may need to respond. That question has become a key issue ahead of the next policy meeting, when policymakers are due to update their interest rate projections after a period in which the rhetoric of many of them leaned hawkish even as the election results, stock markets and other dynamics pointed to a possible slowdown. The problem for markets since the midterm elections "has not been just the prospect of an AI slowdown. It's also been that the Fed has seemingly ignored the risks and uncertainty that the post-election period has brought, and thrown caution to the wind," Macquarie analysts wrote recently. "In a way, Warsh has brought this revolt on himself, by not abandoning his own aversion to expressing forward guidance," even as the debate around what he sees as the signature economic issue of the day has become more complex.
